utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Following yesterday afternoon's discussion about the timing of the trial, the Trial Chamber has decided to take no action on the matter. We were reassured by what was said and we would like to express our gratitude for counsels' continued cooperation with the Trial Chamber in efforts to manage this case efficiently and fairly. We are content to rely on counsels' judgement that the Defence case is on course to be completed in the time allocated. Now, Mr. Ackerman, I understand you have something you wish to raise before the next witness comes into court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness has given two 92 ter statements. I have objection to the second of those, it's 3D01114.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In that statement the witness basically represents himself as an expert on handwriting, and he makes conclusions regarding handwriting comparisons that he's made. And nowhere has it been shown that he has any expertise in that regard, the rules regarding designation of an expert have not been followed in this regard, and therefore I object to that second -- that second statement. And I can point you to the various paragraphs or parts of paragraphs where he does express these opinions as if he were a qualified handwriting expert, if you'd like me to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I've read this and have made certain comments on the page, but some might say that handwriting is one of these things that anyone can make some sort of judgement about and is not exclusively a matter for expertise; however, certain aspects of it may be exclusively matters for expertise. Now, my inclination in these circumstances would be to note your objection and reserve the question of the admissibility of this evidence until we've heard it and then let you address us at the end of the witness's evidence again on the same lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The problem with that, Your Honour, of course is that you would have then heard it and it may be quite difficult to then put it completely out of your minds. I know you're professional Judges and you're supposed to be quite good at that, but it's hard to unring a bell. In any event, I've heard your response and I accept it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There may be parts of this in any event, even if you were right about the -- this being exclusively a matter of expertise, that the witness could say something about. Part of this relates to alteration, I think, and we would then need to apply a pretty artificial approach to hearing the evidence and some of it might be okay. So I'll hear Mr. Stamp or Mr. Hannis, not clear who, on this, and then the Chamber will have a brief discussion. Mr. Stamp. You're not concerned --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have no comment to make except --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Visnjic -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Except that the area of handwriting falls in the -- in a category that is not exclusively for experts. A witness can make his own observations as to what handwriting is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic, anything you wish to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can just say in relation to this witness, or rather, the material that he looked at that it has to do with the material we got a few days ago, quite literally a few days ago. Our intention is to subject this material to expertise, this is a special request that we have, because we don't think it's only a question of handwriting but also some other elements - I'm just say this by way of an example, different pens, the way this was done, and so on and so forth. I believe this also merits special expertise. As I've said, the material indeed arrived only a few days ago. Part of this material we have been trying to obtain for the past two years from the government, or rather, the National Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, anything you wish to say in response to these things? Just before you do, may I say that I am quite surprised sometimes by the difference in various signatures I apply myself and I would hate to have the accuracy of my writing exclusively determined by a layman, so we're well aware of the problem. It sounds as though Mr. Visnjic is conscious of his problem if he wants to go anywhere significant on this without expert evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll just say that in the course of my years in the courtroom I've been on both sides of this issue. I've put on such witnesses and cross-examined such witnesses, and I'd prefer to cross-examine them because I think a lot of what they do is witchcraft almost. So to suggest that a layman might do a better job though than an expert probably is a little much. I think an expert might do a better job than a layman and I'm not sure what a layman says would have any value at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you sound as though you'll have a more-interesting-than-average day in court today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's going to be a great deal more interesting because I left all my papers in my office, so I've got to figure out a way to deal with that also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will proceed as I have indicated, Mr. Ackerman. We'll hear the evidence, we'll let you address us on it if you feel it appropriate, and meanwhile we'll reserve the question of its admissibility, the relevant part of this witness's evidence, until the end of it and your opportunity to address us further. So who is this witness, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our next witness is Colonel Milovan Vlajkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vlajkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning to all of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will now be examined by Mr. Visnjic on behalf of Mr. Ojdanic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: For the record, could you please give your name.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I am Milovan Vlajkovic, a retired army colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you start your testimony I wish to ask you whether it is correct that you gave a statement to the Defence team of General Ojdanic, that you signed on the 17th of August, 2008 [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that during the proofing session you looked at this statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you looked at this statement you told me that you have a change that you would like to make in relation to paragraph 14. I would like to ask you now to tell the Trial Chamber what it is that you would like to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: It's not a change. I am convinced that this paragraph should be spelled out in more precise terms. Its essence is no different. This is how I would like it to read, if you accept it. The first two lines would not be changed. Line 3, after the word "deputy" there would be a comma and the sentence continues as follows.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Like all other documents that he signed." Further on, next paragraph: "Certain documents with the signature of the Chief of General Staff could have been recorded and registered in the organizational unit of the General Staff where they had been drafted, or rather, at the tactical leaders," that is how I would like it to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to this change you didn't have any other objections to the text?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you also confirm for me that you gave yet another statement, an addendum, on the 17th of September, 2007?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you look at the text of the additional statement that you signed?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I reviewed the text and I have no objections in relation to the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, if you were to testify before this court, would you give the same answers as you did in your statement of the 17th of August, 2007, and your additional statement signed on the 17th of September, 2007?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is Defence Exhibits 3D1112, that is the statement dated the 17th of August, 2007, and 3D1114, that is an addendum to the witness's statement and that was signed on the 17th of September, 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, could you tell me what duties you had in 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998 and in 1999 I was chef de cabinet of the Chief of General Staff or from the beginning of the war of the chief of the staff of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the posts held by the witness and also the organs that he headed are described in paragraphs 3 through 5 in 3D1112, so I don't want to go into any further detail now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, tell me, one of the duties that you had, or rather, one of the powers that your organ had was the technical preparation of meetings of the collegium of the Chief of General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to look at 3D666. In your statement you described in detail how the minutes from the collegium were recorded and later typed up, so I don't want to go into any detail now. I would just like to show the Trial Chamber some details that appear in the minutes from the collegium and for the sake of clarification. It is the collegium held on the 8th of June, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In B/C/S page 19, please, and in English page 2. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 18 in the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, could you please tell me us in what kind of a room meetings of the collegium of the Chief of General Staff were held, or rather, what kind of facilities were there for recording and later on for creating the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: As for the period up to the beginning of the war sessions of the collegium were held in the operations room of the General Staff, where there were full technical facilities for recording collegium meetings and later to have the audio recording transcripted. Later on during the course of the war we did not have such possibilities, so minutes were kept at collegium meetings or at briefings, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now, what did the room look like? I would like to know where the meeting -- where the members of the collegium sat, how the recording took place.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The members of the collegium sat in accordance with precedence at a table that was P shaped, the shape of a Cyrillic P. Also there was a screen where slides were projected from the middle of the room. The sound technician who was involved in this work would, once the Chief of General Staff would call out the names, he would establish visually who got the floor and then he would turn on the microphone. It could sometimes happen that he could not locate the speaker straight away, then the microphone would be turned on which caused a lack of clarity in the sound recording. And then the typist could not decipher this, and that is why we see these dots in the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So when we look at this page that is in front of us --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: -- When the typist could not hear what was being said, then there would be dots?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Also sometimes during the course of his speech the speaker would turn his head the other way, the microphone would not pick up what he was saying. Sometimes he would get up to point something out on the screen or someone would disturb the sound recording by speaking at the same time when one speaker was speaking and then the transcript could not be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What other kinds of mistakes came up? You looked at this specific document?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And you noted a mistake in relation to a particular person?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The sound technician had the seating arrangement at the collegium in front of him and that is how he recorded the beginning of the remarks of a particular speaker. However, we at the General Staff have two Ristics, so it is possible that the typist when he saw the last name Ristic as a matter of inertia he wrote Radomir but it was also Svetislav Ristic head of the legal department who attended and briefed the meeting on this particular subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know perhaps what was discussed?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The draft rules of service which is other part of the legal department, they are the tactical mainstay of that activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, during the session there was no special warning that there was an audio recording taking place?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, everybody knew that and the sound technician sat in front of everyone practically.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you have the impression that the participants in the collegium meetings were hesitant in terms of saying something?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I think that they quite openly spoke about the matters that they were conducting the briefings on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 3D706. Your Honours, now I would like to move on to another topic. It is a note from the 15th of March, it is a note on a telephone conversation of Dragoljub Ojdanic, Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, with the NATO Supreme Commander for Europe, General Wesley Clark.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you looked at this document - and I don't want to go into its content - can you just tell us whether you know how this document was compiled?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: After the conversation took place, since this was a telephone conversation and there was simultaneous or consecutive interpretation during the conversation, it is practically the interpreter who compiled the note. In this particular case it was the interpreter, and then the interpreter submitted this to the office, the cabinet, and then it was archived in the register of the office and then the document was further treated in accordance with the orders of the Chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If we look at the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, here we can see that this document was submitted to the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Mr. Slobodan Milosevic; President of the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Milan Milutinovic; President of the federal government, or rather -- this is a mistake -- oh, yes, Mr. Momir Bulatovic, Prime Minister; Minister for Foreign Affairs; and Minister of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have document 3D707. General, what we have before us is the first page of this document, it is a letter with your signature on it. Can you tell us what this is about?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a cover letter concerning the note on the telephone conversation with General Wesley Clark, the NATO commander, and it is with this cover letter that it was sent to the President of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and of the Supreme Defence Council, Mr. Slobodan Milosevic. With the president we primarily communicated through the chef de cabinet of the military cabinet, that is to say General Slavoljub Susic. We particularly paid attention to the following, we wanted to send documents to the president as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this specific case could I please see page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So this is an official note yet again concerning a telephone conversation between General Dragoljub Ojdanic and the NATO Commander for Europe, General Wesley Clark, on the 22nd of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the next page in B/C/S and I think that it's the same in English, the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, we see here from the text that General Clark - and we see that in the first paragraph - asked to General Ojdanic to meet with General Anderson, who was in Belgrade at the time on Richard Holbrooke's delegation, and he had a message from General Clark for General Ojdanic. In the same text in the one-but-last paragraph it says that General Ojdanic --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: -- That that meeting depended on President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what you testified to here, this document was sent straight away to President Milosevic. Do you know whether General Ojdanic and General Anderson actually did meet on the 22nd of March?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say decidedly whether it's a yes or no, I don't know whether they did meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, is 3D707 this document and a covering letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And for 3D706 we simply had the note and no covering letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we don't have the letter, we don't have the cover letter. I assume -- that's the way I got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's simply that the witness's evidence at the outset -- it's clear now, but the witness's evidence suggested that 3D707 was the covering letter for 3D706; that's now been cleared up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Different dates. Thank you. 3D1090, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, the document is coming up. What is this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The document we're looking at is a covering letter from the Ministry of Justice. It concerns a letter by The Hague Prosecutor, Ms. Louise Arbour and this letter is here forwarded to the Chief of the General Staff but there are absolutely no annotations or instructions as to what to do with it next. As soon as the letter was received by the cabinet on the 2nd of May, 1999, it was filed, archived pursuant to orders of the Chief of the General Staff was further processed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, just a single question. This letter by Ms. Louise Arbour, the date it bears is the 26th of March, 1999, however, the justice ministry forwarded it to the General Staff only as late as the 29th of April, 1999, or at least that is borne out by the date on this document. When in actual fact did the General Staff receive this letter?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: There is one thing that you can base an assumption like that on and that is the filing stamp or the incoming stamp, and the stamp shows the date the 2nd of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You mean the one in the lower right corner?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I mean, that is the stamp of the chef de cabinet of the Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: My next question --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we pull up the B/C/S, please. Up, please, not zoom in. [In English] A little bit more. [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You see this document, there are two handwritten notes on it jotted down on the face of the document. Can you tell us what those are about?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The tactical leader and mainstay, in this case the legal administration, the chief of that particular administration, as soon as he receives a document, normally he writes down by hand what the document is supposed to be subjected to next. You see that Nikolic here who was the chief of that sector as soon as the 3rd of May forwarded this to the legal administration and said that the orders of the Chief of the General Staff should be followed, and then there is a further note on the right-hand side which says "urgent." The deadline for the order, if I'm not mistaken, was the 4th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have the document back, the lower portion of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In the lower half of this page we see a typewritten note. Can you tell us what it says.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: During the technical processing of documents, it was the established practice for the notes and the order itself of the Chief of the General Staff to be conveyed in this form, usually it was in the lower half of the page and the document was here submitted to the legal section, sector, and they were told to draft an order to take appropriate measures, the deadline being the 4th of May, 1999. This shows how urgent it was for the Chief of the General Staff to react to this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, this is the letter by Louise Arbour that was attached, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes,.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now have 3D1091.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before we depart from that document, your concentration just now is on the 3rd of May, which may not be what really matters. Mr. Vlajkovic, who was Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nikolic at the time was the chief of the legal administration. I'm not sure if my time-line is all right, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that -- by that do you mean the Ministry of Justice or do you mean the office of the Chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no -- yes, I mean the administration of the Chief of the General Staff, because he implemented his orders through his own organizational units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, surely what matters here is the date that the Ministry of Justice got the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as far as my client's interest is concerned, what matters is when he received the document; and if you look at this document you see that it wasn't forwarded to him before the 2nd, him or his service. What I'm trying to represent here is what he did when he received document, what his reaction was, and it is my intention to show another four or five documents relating to that. I don't know why this document wasn't sent by the Ministry of Justice before the 29th of April, and I don't know how Louise Arbour ever sent this letter to the justice ministry, and most of all I don't know why the letter took an entire month to reach my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vlajkovic, on the document there is a stamp and there is a handwritten number and a date, the 29th of April. What is that referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you mean the stamp in the upper right corner?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The justice ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Are you qualified to tell us what that refers to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, considering how we deal with documents, this is the stamp of the Ministry of Justice, and it says that on the 29th of April the letter was filed and further processed. I base my assumption on rules that we apply when we deal with documents of this kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do you use a similar stamp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see our stamp in the lower left-hand corner of the document, where you see the stamp of the chief of the cabinet of the Chief of the General Staff, and you have our number, our final file number there too as well as the date when the document was filed, when it was entered into the register and when it received the cabinet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic, please proceed to the next number -- the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D1091, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, this is another letter, I see the date, the 5th of May, 1999. What sort of a letter is this? This is a document that you signed, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was the usual mode of communication between me as chef de cabinet and the assistant chiefs of the General Staff. Specifically this is what the letter is about. When the legal sector submitted a draft order to the chief for inspection, he would then forward this to his deputy and the assistant for operations and staff affairs, General Blagoje Kovacevic. He submitted the draft to them in order to get their opinions, and this was about taking measures to prevent war crimes in this specific case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is 3D1092.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, another document, the date appears to be the 6th of May, 1999, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Briefly, what is its relation to the previous document?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: This is about objections raised in relation to the draft order by the deputy Chief of the General Staff and the assistant for operations and staff affairs. I sent this to the legal sector of the administration for recruitment, mobilisation, and system-related issues. I said that they should enter this into their draft and then bring the whole document back to the chief for his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document, please, 3D483.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This is an order by the Chief of Staff of the general -- of the Supreme Command, Dragoljub Ojdanic, the 10th of May, 1999. Colonel, you inspected this document, didn't you? Is this document a result of objections and work done on the draft, the draft from the previous document?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: After all the stages as the document was being drafted, this was eventually the final document that the chief signed off. The document was then duly forwarded to subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless I'm mistaken there is an attachment containing another letter by Ms. Louise Arbour, this is 3D708 -- excuse me, 3D788. My apologies. Before we start with this, can we please have the previous document back, 3D483. If we could please have page 2 in the B/C/S and then page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, there was an attachment to this document selected sections of the Geneva Conventions; that's what it contained, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The title would indicate that this is the document, but I don't remember the attachment. It was the legal sector and the sector for recruitment and mobilisation that were in charge of distributing the order and I wasn't familiar of the entire substance of the parcel, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go back to the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What about the lower left corner of this list, what is it exactly? What's the list in the lower left corner?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of every document there is a list of units that the document is submitted to; in this case, the army command, the 1st, the 2nd, and the 3rd PVO, the navy, organization of units of the staff of the Supreme Command, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What about the stamp in the lower left corner?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the 3rd Army stamp. This means they received the document, they gave it a file number on the date stated, which right now is illegible to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I think this is the 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I can't see the whole page, can I?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at another document, 3D788.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Colonel, this is another document from the Federal Ministry of Justice; it was sent to the Supreme Command of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the same letter, Ms. Louise Arbour. That same day and under the same file number, it was sent by the Ministry of Justice and it was accompanied by a letter that was sent to the Chief of the General Staff and that's how it eventually reached the cabinet. This is the same letter that was sent to two different addresses: General Pavkovic, the 3rd Army commander; and Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next document, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you go off that, I can't say I'm following this particular part. This is sent by whom to whom, Mr. Vlajkovic? Who sent this letter and who did it go to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Ministry of Justice sent two copies of the letter, one addressed to the Chief of the General Staff and the second addressed to the 3rd Army commander under the same number in the same envelope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The one we're looking at says: "Yugoslav Army Supreme Command."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know why it says that it's the Supreme Command, for what reason. General Pavkovic at the time was commander of the 3rd Army, so probably in the Ministry of Justice they didn't know the essence of the relationships and the command relations within the army. This is quite possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did General Pavkovic perhaps have a role in the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what I know, no. As the commander of the 3rd Army, he was subordinated to the Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That may be officially the position, but I'm asking you whether he had a particular role at this stage in the conflict in the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for me his official function is what applies; as for the other roles and functions he may have played, well, I don't know. It's not up to me to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's up to you to comment if you know, if you have knowledge of any role that he played at the Supreme Command, then we should hear about it. We're trying to get the whole picture, and it's not good enough to say this is how it should work in theory; we want to know what happened in practice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in the process of decision-making in the army, the supreme commander, or at the time the president of the Supreme Defence Council, issued orders and directives to the Chief of the General Staff. The Chief of the General Staff with his assistants would implement those decisions, and General Pavkovic at the time was commander of the army. And by the nature of that post, he was not a member of the Supreme Command. I really don't know how he could have been involved in the composition of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which raises the question why on earth was this letter sent to the Supreme Command and in particular General Pavkovic. You can't answer that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't want to speculate. If it was a question of what the Ministry of Justice knew or didn't know, that could be one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps we can clarify this. I would like to look at 3D1092. Let's look at that again. Can we have it on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, let's clarify whether this was something that somebody from the Ministry of Justice knew or didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D1092 -- 90.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 3D1090.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we please look at the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, what post here is given for General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: He is addressed here as the chief of the Supreme Command of the Army of Yugoslavia, which also sounds to me now here very odd.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why does it sound odd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, because there is no chief of the Supreme Command in our - let me say - jargon. There is the supreme commander and there is the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command. There is no chief of the Supreme Command. If I may be allowed to comment. Obviously in the justice ministry they were not familiar with the scheme or the relationships as they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. 3D789, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, we see in front of us a document from the Chief of Staff cabinet of the 14th of May, 1999, which you signed. Can you please tell us briefly what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: According to the order of the Chief of the General Staff that all documents or acts be sent to him that deal with the broader issue of prevention of war crimes, we sent this letter to the organizational unit, where we specified the request of the Chief of the General Staff in that sense. You can see who this document is addressed to on the second page, most probably, the second page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, to the left there is the list of the organizational units to which the cabinet document was sent or to whom the order was conveyed of the Chief of the General Staff on how to act.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 3D790, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document of the 3rd Army command. It's a reply to unfounded charges by the Prosecutor of the International Tribunal and it's been sent to the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, when was this document received at the Supreme Command Staff, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: There is a filing stamp in the lower left-hand corner. I can't see quite clearly, but it seems to be May 1999. You cannot see the left part of the document clearly. Yes, in the English version it's the 27th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This number in the lower left-hand corner, 190-3, what does that signify?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: It's the filing number in the cabinet's filing system under which this document has been stored, so it's related to document 190-1, -2, and -3 because it dealt with the same topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at 3D again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you do that can we go back to the first page of that, please. This relates to other material from the Tribunal; is that right, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, this refers to the letter of Madam Louise Arbour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the letter of the 26th of March. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If we can look at this page now, Colonel, we see that in the reference there is a document that is cited.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The reference document is 190-2, which refers to the order and the letter which was passed to the command of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you say "order," you are thinking of the order for the prevention of humanitarian rights violations?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, precisely, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. I asked you about the order on the prevention of humanitarian law [as interpreted] 3D483.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again and for the last time I would like to look at 3D1090.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm interested in the filing number under which this document was stored in this staff.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: 190-1. When it arrived at the cabinet it was filed in the register as 190-1, meaning that that was the first document, entry document, with that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, we have document 190-2, that is the letter sent to the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And finally we have the response from the 3rd Army filed as document 190-3; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What is the connection between these two documents in terms of content?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The three documents are all about the same topic, the same source document. According to the rules of office procedure and that filing system, the system is permitted and makes it easier to find documents that are immediately related.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to look at 3D639. Now we're moving to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This is a briefing of the 7th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at page 3 in B/C/S. Your Honours, can we please look at page 3 in B/C/S. The translation in English is something that we already had problems with already. I was informed by my assistant that the CLSS corrected the earlier translation. It was corrected as the 7th of April and we will enter it into the system tomorrow, but we just need some -- one reference from this document and Colonel Vlajkovic's explanation in relation to the document. Page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It seems to be already there, the date of the 7th of April is on the English copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, CLSS sent us a translation of this document of the 7th of April, but when we were checking, we established that there was a certain confusion or wrong markings, and they sent a corrected translation tomorrow which has not been entered into the system. But we just want to refer to one part of this document now. Can we please look at page 3 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Sir, you went to these evening briefings during the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Were you present at all of them, at most of them?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I could say that I was present at a large part of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I found one reference on page 3 where there is a note about what you said which says: "Review of sentences to read inside and to keep a diary of the assignments." Can you please tell us what this is about?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: There was a discussion over the previous days or in previous speeches about the members of the army who had been processed for war crimes and committed crimes and to inform the units and the public in more detail about this. So what I said was not really recorded quite correctly, but my proposal had to do with having the information about the perpetrators of crimes announced to the units, the members of the units, where these crimes were committed. I think that this was defined in that way as an assignment by the Chief of the General Staff later.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to move to a different topic that has to do with the additional statement by the witness. If possible - and I was told that it was - I would like to have in the e-court at the same time the B/C/S versions of two exhibits, P1549 and 3D1106. Your Honours, P1549 is a document that the Prosecution used in the proceedings against my client. It's -- and the document 3D1106 is a document which we received, as I already said, from -- [In English] I'm sorry, P1459. It's my mistake. [Interpretation] P1459.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think you should roll it up. Roll it back down. The numbers at the top are of some significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you looked at both documents?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what the documents in question are.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a document of the 3rd Army command drafted at the forward command post, and it refers to the resubordination of units and organs of the Serbian MUP. So it's a report of the 3rd Army command on the implementation of that assignment sent to the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us, in the upper right-hand corner of this exhibit, 3D1106, we see a stamp -- or actually we see two stamps. Can you please tell us what this is about?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The stamp is not on the left copy of the document which is actually the same, and strictly confidential documents should -- I don't see the stamp, but if it's marked with "permanently keep," then that would be the office stamp and confirmation that that document should be placed in the archives and that it must not be destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move to page 2 of this document in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While we're moving, may I just make an inquiry? I noticed that at line 27 -- at page 27, line 17, counsel was indicating where he got 3D1106 from and then there are some dots indicating that maybe the interpreter didn't pick it up. I'm wondering if he said it and it wasn't picked up on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where did you say you had received 3D1106 from, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, 3D1106 is a document that I received from the government through a conclusion of the National Council, which is also an exhibit in the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague tells me that the number of the document with which the government submitted this to me is 3D1104.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now you have both versions of page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- The pages were the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: We don't have it, Your Honour. It should be ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have to see the whole of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we scroll them both down because I would like to see the stamp that is in the lower right-hand corner, or rather, left-hand corner, both versions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, tell me, on document 3D1106 we see a stamp where we see a number and the date. Can you tell me what kind of a stamp this is, what the number is, and what the date is?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: It is the filing stamp of the cabinet of the Supreme Command Staff, and the number, the filing number, is 248-2, which means that in the files of the cabinet it was filed under that number on the 26th of May. On the left copy, we do not see that stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When a document is prepared in a military cabinet, any one, what is the procedure, in how many copies is it made? Where are the originals kept?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: In principle and according to regulations, it is customary practice that the Chief of General Staff signs one copy which then represents the original and which is kept in the archives. After the document is signed by the Chief of General Staff or by a certain officer in charge, a filing stamp is put in the files and a number is registered. The document is copied in the required number of copies, depending on who it is going to be submitted to, and then a stamp is placed on every one of these copies. As a rule, as for the original that is kept in the archives, the stamp would be put and did not have to be put on the original, it depends on where the document would be distributed further and in how many copies. So the practice was that the document would be signed by a certain officer, but only the original. So it's just one signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now move on to document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, it must be a translation problem. The document is -- this is line 4. "The document is copied in the required number of copies and then a stamp is placed on every one of these copies." And then he goes on to say: "As a rule, as for the original, that is kept in the archives, the stamp would be put and did not have to be put on the original, it depends on where the document would be distributed further ..." So the evidence is the stamp goes on copies and it doesn't go on the original; is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He did not say that decidedly. He said: As a rule that was the way it was, but he did not rule out the possibility of having it placed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And where is the signature on this -- is there a signature of a member of staff on one of these? Mr. Vlajkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood your question correctly, the signature is that of the commander, but what is visible here -- I beg your pardon, that both copies were signed by the commander, General Nebojsa Pavkovic. It is obvious that on the right-hand copy there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought we were talking about what happened when the document was received in the office of the Chief of the General Staff when you told us that it would be signed either by the Chief of the General Staff or one of his staff. Well, that's what the English version is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I can go through all of this with the witness again through shorter questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the relevance of what the Chief of the General Staff does unless it's to a document which he is receiving in this instance?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it isn't relevant. The witness was supposed to speak in principle, at one point in time he mentioned the Chief of the General Staff and that is what created the confusion. So if I may go through all of this again with the witness with just a few questions and then we will clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, please, where the document is produced, what is the procedure? How many copies are made? Who signs the copies? And what happens then with the signed copy? Let us start with the text that is typed up and it comes before an authorised official or the commander for signature.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you allow me briefly, the question was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think this witness is qualified to testify as to procedures that go on in 3rd Army headquarters, which he seems to be trying to do. I think he has no competence in that regard. He was never there, he has no idea what they do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I asked the witness to explain to us how this is being done in principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, he must relate his evidence to what happened in this case. What happened in the office of the Chief of General Staff is at first sight irrelevant to what might have happened in the office of the commander of the 3rd Army. So you would have to set a foundation for this witness giving evidence about what happened in the offices of the 3rd Army. And he might well be able to do that, I can think of ways, but perhaps you could establish that foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am making a foundation on the basis of office practice and rules in terms of document creation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on just now. Mr. Vlajkovic, could you please leave the courtroom with the usher while we deal with this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Tell me why you think what happens in the office of the Chief of the General Staff is relevant to what happens in the office of the 3rd Army commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because, Your Honour, the administration works in the same way and in a similar way in all offices in the military. I can -- and there are also regulations regarding this. You will see in this specific case that there are many small details that can lead to the conclusion that we will probably resolve ultimately through expertise, but in this way I'm trying to indicate that there are many unusual details in relation to these documents that ultimately will result, most probably, in expertise. But it is simply impossible to encounter that many coincidences in one single place. One of them is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're departing from the question that we're trying to deal with. I understand what you're trying to do overall, but I need to know the relevance of what happens in one office to events in another, especially since we've already had answers which indicate that not a uniform practice is followed in the office of the Chief of the General Staff. Now, how will this witness know what goes on in the office of the commander of the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. On that, I fully agree with Mr. Ackerman, he doesn't know that. He doesn't know that, but he knows which way they're supposed to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How can we know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the regulations are the same for the functioning of all offices in the military. There are rules of office work regulating that in the army. One knows exactly how a document is filed, why it is filed, how a document is produced, where a stamp is placed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where are the rules then?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, I think -- well, I'm not sure. Perhaps the Prosecutor exhibited this -- these rules, but if they haven't then we will. Now I'm told that they have been exhibited and that there is a P number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know the P number?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, if you ... [Interpretation] If you give me a bit of time, I will be able to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps we should break now and give you time to organize this, but we can read these rules for ourselves without necessarily hearing from somebody about what goes on in his office when we're dealing with what goes on in another office. So you could perhaps concentrate on how much of this needs to be led from the witness. You may also consider establishing with him a basis for saying that something ought to have been done in another office of which he has no direct experience. And if these rules are found in the next few minutes, it would be helpful if we could have a copy of them during the break. We'll resume at ten to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we've looked at our documents and the rules on official correspondence is P1548, it's an OTP exhibit, and it has been admitted. Secondly, I went through the documents and I followed your instructions, indeed. I will not be asking the witness to tell me about the procedure applied by the 3rd Army. We shall focus in his evidence on how documents were processed in the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If it's relevant, I have no objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- As to how they're processed in the General Staff, it probably is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For a different reason, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: For a different reason, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's proceed. Bring the witness back, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vlajkovic, we have dealt with the legal issue and we can now proceed with the evidence. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vlajkovic, before we proceed I showed you a while ago 3D790, if you remember that was General Pavkovic's response that he sent to the Supreme Command Staff and it was about the Louise Arbour letter. This document was received on the 27th of May, at least based on the incoming stamp, 27th of May, 1999, and the date that the document bears, which is apparently when the document was produced, is the 17th of May, 1999. Based on your experience, based on what sort of parcels or letters you were receiving from the 3rd Army at the time, can you please compare 3D790 and 3D1106. The date the document was produced it appears based on this document is the 25th of May, 1999, and the day it was filed appears to be the 26th of May, 1999. Can you comment on that, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Obviously these are two different points in time, some distance apart. The time the document took to get from the 3rd command to the Supreme Command Staff. In the first case the time is ten days and in the other case it's a single day, and I can't speculate as to what might have caused this delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness now please be shown 3D1109, page 1 of that document, please. Your Honours, this is the register, the cabinet register, of the chief of the Supreme Command Staff in relation to 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before we go to that, you're moving rather quickly through this. 790 is the response to Arbour and it was produced on the 25th, is that right, and gets there on the 26th; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D790 was produced on the 17th of May, 1999, and it got there on the 27th of May, whereas 3D1106 was produced on the 25th of May, 1999, and apparently reached its destination on the 26th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D1109, please. Can the witness please be shown the document. We only have a single copy of this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, what does page 1 of this document tell you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a title page of the register of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command and the date is 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have pages 2 and 3 shown at the same time, split screens in e-court. Page 2 on the left and page 3 on the right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, can you briefly explain what these columns are about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for the translation. I will need a special request for CLSS, they normally refuse to translate handwritten documents; therefore, there will need to be a special ruling for this to be translated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You want me to explain what the columns are about, right? The first is the register number, the number under which a document is entered into the register. The next one is relevant referential numbers. Documents that have to do with this can be filed under certain numbers, 1, 2, 3, 4, the date of receipt, the addressee, the substance of the document, who received it, and until which time it must be kept. So these are the columns that one normally uses when receiving a document like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So 248, column 248, for example, can we please zoom in on column 248 on both pages. The other document, too, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Column 248, this is the register number, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: We looked a while ago at 3D1106 and its file or register number was 248-2. Colonel, is that consistent with the entry in the register?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The entry under number 2, the 26th of May, says: "Document by the 3rd Army command sent from the forward command post," their own file number, 872-94, and then brief description of substance, what its about, resubordination of MUP units on that day, a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What about column 8, please, it says: "Name of organ" and the entry we see there is a surname, right, whose surname?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Mine, meaning this document was dispatched from that office and forwarded to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, have you ever seen the document by the 3rd Army command 872-94/1-2?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: If we're talking about this particular time-period, I can't be specific, I can't say yes and I can't say no. I looked at the substance of specific documents only to the extent that it was necessary for me to present the chief with what a certain document was about and in order to make calls as to how documents would be further processed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, can you tell me which document is recorded above this document, the date being the 15th of May, 1999, to the extent that you find this legible or decipherable.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: One can sort of see what it's about it, Federal Ministry of Defence, administration for preparing republican organs for defence. As for its substance, it's a note, it's a note from a meeting of the Chief of the General Staff, a meeting held in that administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does it have a number in column 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the far right there are some figures that can barely be seen, but I can't decipher them based on this copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do documents in a sequence, as you have described them in your statement, have numbers such as 94/1-2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a number that was created at the spot of the creation of the document. It was at the forward command post of the 3rd Army, and the number given was 872-94/1-2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is that the number that we've seen already on 3D1106?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: We'll be coming back to this document later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what I'm about to show the witness now is a document that we believe is document 248-1, a defence ministry official note, the Exhibit Number is 3D1105. Can the witness be shown that document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you've had a look, haven't you. This is an official note by the federal defence ministry. Can you tell us something about the date and the number that the document bears, the number under which it was dispatched by the defence ministry.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: This is an official note produced during the visit made by the chief of the Supreme Command Staff to the administration for preparations of republican organs for defence. It is obvious here that the number in their register was 01-53/99, and the date is the 7th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the last page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, can you comment on the stamp, date, and number in the lower left corner of 3D1105.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: When the note reached the cabinet, it was filed in the cabinet's register on the 15th of May, and the number was 248, this was the first or initial document in that particular file.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, you've had a chance to go through the document and look at it closely, 3D1105 and 3D1106, both these documents. What about their substance, is there a link between the two documents? Is there anything that might constitute a reason for these two different documents to be filed under the same register number?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Having inspected both documents, I failed to notice any reason at all for these to be filed in this way in the cabinet's register by using the same number in reference to both. As a matter of principle, this can only be done with documents that talk about the same subject matter, such as the Louise Arbour letter, 190/1, /2, and /3.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can you please go back to Exhibit Number 3D1109, pages 2 and 3. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at column 10 which is the last column in this row or sequence, I'm talking about 248, those documents, can you explain what this stamp means in column 10 and what the handwritten portion says.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the column where one records how long a document is meant to be kept for, above the stamp you see "keep permanently," and then it says: "Military archive of the VJ" and the number begins with 21, and then it's followed probably by 606 but I'm not certain. What this means is that the document was submitted to the military archive, I mean the original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So what's this number over here 21606?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: This number marks the list, the archive list of documents submitted to the military archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is this the so-called archive list, as you referred to it, that's what the document is called, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, both these documents were registered and bearing in mind column 10, would this not mean that both these documents were submitted to the military archive and they are to be found in 21606, which is a file which is in the archive?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: As a rule, as a matter of principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, 3D1108 is our next exhibit. My apologies. While we still have this before us, these two pages, page 3 on the right -- could we scroll further to the right, please. To the right, just a little. Move the image as far as the right-hand edge or end of the page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, if I look at column 10 I see a number of signatures there next to the archive file numbers. Whose signatures are these?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D1108, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Fortunately in this case we have a translation. Can you just explain briefly about the stamp in the upper left corner of this document.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: As per normal, there is a stamp in the upper left corner of whoever produced the document in a manner of speaking, and in this case as it happens, it's the Chief of Staff of the cabinet of the Supreme Command Staff and this is the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The 10th of August, 1999, is the date we see there, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ immediately after the end of command operations issue an order from all of the war-related documents to be submitted and kept in the VJ archive?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew at the time that I would be leaving the cabinet and I agreed with the chief and the assistant that the assistant should take care of this and take it from there. So the assistant analysed the way in which the documents were to be submitted to the military archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And who was your deputy at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Milan Radojcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the top right-hand corner, what do these numbers represent, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the information from the military archive on the date of receipt, the quantity of received material, and the registered number -- register number in their books, most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 2 of this document, please. I'm interested in number 82.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, can you please explain what is stated here in this column marked with 82, what is the significance of the text in column 3?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The text in column 3 is the full name of the document registered as 248-1, it's an official note from a meeting between the chief of Supreme Command Staff and the chief of administration for the preparation of the Republican organs for the defence. It's a document --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. That is the document that we showed a little bit earlier, Exhibit 3D1105.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, what is marked in column 4 of this archive list?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: That's the number under which the document is filed in the cabinet register where it was created.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what do you see in column 4 in this case?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: You can see that document 248-2 was added without citing the contents of the document in the third column.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please now comment on columns 5 and 6 also in this entry marked 82 some things were crossed out here, some numbers.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: A change was made so that instead of one document, number 2 is written; and instead of a total of three pages, there are a total of five pages. This is the only case that I've seen here that the correction was made both in the number of the document and the number of pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me when you in the cabinet prepared the documents, packed them for archiving.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just one correction, page 44, line 4, the B/C/S said: Both the number of documents, not the number of document. It might make a difference as to how it's understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, in the cabinet when you packed the documents in order to hand them over to the military archive, what does it look like physically? What -- what is that? How do you do that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The head of the office with the archive list and the attached documents that are prepared goes to the military archive, and with the person from the military archive checks over each document and checks it against the archive list that the number of the document is correctly written and the number of the pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And now please tell me in case --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: In case that there is something that does not agree, then a correction is made in the presence of the person from the cabinet, and this correction means that the document is received with those particular characteristics.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When we look at these pages of the archive list in front of us, we see that corrections were made sometimes in column 5, sometimes in column 6 also.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Am I correct if I say that the only column where corrections were made or the only instance where corrections were made in both columns, so regarding the number of documents and the number of pages, is column marked 82 where document numbered 248-2 was added; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the last page of this document, that would be 3D1108.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's keep the whole page in view and we can't see the whole Serbian version, the entire page. We would like to be able to look at the full page, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, at the bottom there are two signatures. Can you tell us whose signatures these are.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The person who drafted the list, warrant officer, Jovanovic Miodrag was the chief of the office of the General Staff; and then on the right it was Colonel Milan Radojcic, or rather, Vlajkovic Milovan, but according to my information that work was actually done by my deputy Colonel Radojcic, and he signed the archive list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So this signature here at the bottom is not your signature?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: We have here written PO, "po ovlascenju"?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this can be seen in the B/C/S. It is covered over the stamp but it is clear, probably in the English version, probably the translators did not pay attention to that particular detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
