utterances.text: Colonel, what I would like to know now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The English version does deal with it, I think, it says it's signed for the chief, Colonel Vlajkovic, and then says a signature and a stamp, and the signature could not be read by an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, yes, I see it now. Thank you. I apologise to the translators. It's very good that they noted this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested now is at the bottom on the right-hand corner there is a text there. Can you please tell us what it says there and who is the person who wrote that entry.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: In the right-hand corner there is a note by the person from the military archive who received the material in question, specifically it was warrant first -- warrant first -- officer first class Dusan Stanojevski, if I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: According to your knowledge, according to practice, who actually reviews and makes corrections of these documents, is that the person who receives the documents or is it someone else?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Corrections are made only by the person who receives the document in the presence of a person from our side, and they certify that the archive list was definitely received with the made corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You made a comment saying that the way the numbers are written, 248-2, does not correspond to, let's say, the handwriting that the other corrections are made in, in this document. Can you please tell us a little bit more, how you reached that conclusion. Can you add something to what you said.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Entry number 82 has a correction where number 2 is written. This is on page 2 of the document and the numbers written are 248-2. The way this is written is different from the way the other changes are entered on that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like you to look at Exhibit 4D135. I would like to ask you to look at this whole document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a hard copy. Perhaps we can just give it to the witness to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that we worked on this analysis, that the analysis was made in the Supreme Command Staff, and that is that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, everything that you know about the way the Supreme Command Staff worked, the document that we discussed today throughout the day, 3D1106, and in view of its content, were you included or participated in this analysis that includes all the requests sent to the Supreme Command Staff by the 3rd Army command?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The methodology of work of the Supreme Command Staff would definitely include such a document because all the requests of the 3rd command were there, were covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, let me ask you this: You attended many meetings of the collegium, the evening briefings, and some other documents and so on. Did you ever hear any conversation or any plan to expel Kosovo Albanians from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear General Ojdanic at any point speaking about the expulsion of Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that General Ojdanic did anything or said anything at any point that would indicate that he was prejudiced towards Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: No also to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You were chef de cabinet at the time of General Perisic also and during the term of office of General Ojdanic. Can you please tell us your opinion - you had the opportunity to work with General Ojdanic - to tell us your opinion about his characteristics as a commander and as a person, as a man.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Like I said in my statement, this is a person of exceptional professional abilities, and through training and work he came to this position which implies professional, moral, and human characteristics of a specific type, so I would have nothing to add to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us anything in terms of the following. General Ojdanic as a person, is he an open, direct, informal person?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: This is how I thought about him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honours. I apologise for exceeding my time, but I had to go through the documents in detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I first would like the usher to take this packet of documents to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Colonel Vlajkovic, we're going to be talking about some documents, and to make it easier for you I've prepared that group of documents that I'll be referring to because moving through them on the screen tends to be tedious at times and slow things down, so maybe we can speed up just a little bit with you looking at them that way. I'm John Ackerman; I represent General Pavkovic in this case. In your original statement to Mr. Visnjic when you set out what you've done in your career, you told us that during the second half of 1998 and the first half of 1999 you were the chef de cabinet or chief of office to General Ojdanic, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what was your rank at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was the same rank you retired with?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you were the chief of office for General Ojdanic, you -- you spoke in your statement about a number of the duties that you had, and I'd like to run through them very quickly so you can correct me if I've got them wrong. Excuse me just a second. You said that among those duties were the provision of financial, technical, and physical conditions for work, servicing the chief and the deputy Chief of the General Staff. So you -- you basically worked for both General Ojdanic and his deputy?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, or to be more precise was responsible for tasks relating to the deputy Chief of the General Staff, which was performed at the time by Stankovic, who was then in charge of jobs of the deputy Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. You also said that you -- that this involved carrying out a number of operational, planning, protocol, legal, personal, financial, security, and similar tasks. Could you tell us what the operational tasks that you performed were.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: What's been just mentioned, this is an informal title. For example, operations jobs had to do with the preparation of mail for signature, its distribution, so by plan they had to do with the development of the plan of work of the Chief of the General Staff; then in protocol terms that had to do with visits, whether they went on visits or received them, and this was generally done by desk officers for protocol personnel and financial tasks were also conducted in the cabinet, by the cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What about legal, personal, security?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The legal affairs officer at the cabinet mostly dealt with the documents and matters that had to do with legal affairs, the protection of civilian affairs or responding to requests that were sent to the cabinet. Personnel, of course we had personnel records, this was also done by an officer at the cabinet for members of the cabinet. He took care of promotions, elements of the salaries, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The personal part, should that be translated as personnel instead of personal; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: When I speak about personnel, we are thinking persons, individuals, when they have the right to certain rights and privileges, when they cease, these have to do with certain salary categories or ranks, so it has to do with personal matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You didn't perform actually personal tasks for the general like picking up his laundry and doing personal things for him, you were dealing with personnel matters. I think there's a translation issue there, isn't there, because the English says "personal" rather than "personnel."

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The Chief of the General Staff, it would be ridiculous if I did his laundry. I don't know where that question comes from. What I meant under personnel and cadre matters, what I meant was orders and things that had to do with the aspects of that particular job, and those are the frameworks that I moved in within the parameters of that job.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What was the security part of it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Trips of Chief of the General Staff implied certain security aspects, the security department that functioned in the General Staff in a way covered that, and I was the one who coordinated that with them, when and where he would be travelling, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 of your statement you say that the office drafted a monthly work-plan. Was the drafting of that plan also part of your job?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Ultimately, yes, because I would take the plan of work to the chief and I would be responsible for its accuracy, the accuracy and the tasks that were being implemented. It could be drafted in the cabinet. There was the deputy who could work on it or one of the desk officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In paragraph 10 you say that it was your job to collect and prepare the mail, and this may be another translation issue, but what it says in the English that you collected and prepared the mail to be signed by the members of the General Staff, NGS. Is that true, you handled the mail for all of the members of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, only for the Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this mail was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, NGS is the Chief of the General Staff, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Maybe I misunderstood that, Your Honour. It's entirely possible since my Serbian isn't all that great.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You say the Chief of the General Staff looked over and signed the mail twice a day, so you would collect and prepare the mail for him two times each day and bring it to his attention for signature, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You also tell us that you regularly attended sessions of the collegium and afterwards it was your job to frame in detail and stylised language the tasks emerging from those meetings and see that they were typed and properly distributed, correct? That's paragraph 11.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you also monitored the implementation of tasks and reported your findings to the Chief of the General Staff, and I take it that you prepared him for the briefing that he did in that regard at the beginning of each session of the collegium.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood the question correctly, I didn't prepare him for the briefing at the beginning of the collegium, but in the course of the collegium, during the entire collegium, I would be informing him about the degree to which the tasks were implemented and I would establish that before the collegium meeting would begin in contacts either with the deputies or those who were in charge of implementing particular assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, I think we understand. Your job was to follow-up on those tasks and then let the -- let General Ojdanic know how they were being followed?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: To inform him if the assignments were implemented or at what stage of implementation they were, other than about assignments that I was in charge of monitoring.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And finally in paragraph 5 you point out that the nature, complexity, scope, and content of the work demanded all-day engagement of the chief, his associates, assistants, and office, and I take it that that included you, that you were extraordinarily busy and the work demanded your all-day engagement?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: As for me, I was graded by my superior, in this case it was the Chief of the General Staff, General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There's been some kind of a misunderstanding. My question had to do with the nature of the work. It required your attention on an all-day basis, did it not, very complex, very busy?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I was informed that the all-day part of my question really wasn't appropriately translated to you, but I think we have it now. I want you to look at a couple of documents. First take a look at 3D1108, and I just have a preliminary question or two to ask you about that document. If I wanted to go -- this is kept in an archive somewhere, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean military archives or the files of the cabinet?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what I mean. I'm asking you. Where is this kept? What kind of an archive is it kept in? Where is it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what we've been saying so far, this is a document that is in the archive list under number 82 and 248 is the filing number in the cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think you understand my question at all. Look at the first page of this document. In the upper right-hand corner there's a stamp, that stamp says something about the archive, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. I really have to ask what document you're asking me about. The command of the 3rd Army? 872-84, there is no stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Look at your screen, the document is 3D1108.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if you look at the tabs you'll see 3D1108, it's about one, two -- it's about the fifth document in your list, in your book there.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I'm trying to find out --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- Is where this document is kept. There's an archive stamp on it, and I want to know where that archive is.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Those archives are in Zelenik, a Belgrade municipality, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If I wanted to go to that archive and see this document, I couldn't just walk in and start going through the archives and looking for it, can I?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you go to the archive and go through the archives and look at this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think I could go just like that, without approval from the officer in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you'd have to ask for approval to get in and look at this document, and I take it if you got approval and went in to look at it then that would be recorded somewhere and we'd know that you went and looked at it and what you looked at and how long you were there and so forth, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: As for these technical details related to going to the archives, recording the persons who entered, the time they spent there, I'm not aware of any of that and I cannot give an unequivocal answer as to how all of that would go; however, if it is based on a request, then the request is certainly recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I take it that in preparation for your testimony here, you did not go to the archive and look at the original documents in the archive, but what you saw was what lawyer Visnjic wanted you to see, what he handed you, not the actual document in the archive?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I saw the documents that were provided to me by Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, if you will look at this document, this 3D1108 that we're looking at, I see on the first page that we have documents 1 through 6, and then if you go to the second page it skips to document 79. What happened to the records for documents 7 through 78?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The real address for this question is Mr. Visnjic. Don't make me speculate as to whether he needed that or not, whether it was of interest to him or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you never saw entries number 7 through 78 I take it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to look, if you will, at 3D1109 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one point that should be noted, I think, is that the translation has 6 at the top of that page, but in the original items 1 to 6 are on the first page. And therefore, there's no link necessarily, just in case we're misled later, no link necessarily between 6 and then 79.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think what you mean by "link."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you're looking at the gap, but the suggestion of the witness is that Mr. Visnjic may only have asked for certain pages of this document, and the English version is misleading because it puts number 6 on the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it's something not to lose sight of.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The original ends with 6 on the first page and starts with 77 on the second.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at 3D1109 now, and this is the one we don't have an English translation of, which is unfortunate because it makes it difficult for all of us to deal with it. But if you'll look at this document, it begins with the number 247, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The copy starts with 247, but the original register that is in the cabinet, of course, starts with number 1 and it ends at the end of the year with a certain number, end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in preparation for your testimony here today, did you review all of those pages, 1 through the end, whatever the end number is, or did you just look at this one page?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: While preparing for my testimony, I looked only at the pages that were provided to me in copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Take a look at the top there at document 247, you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if I'm reading Serbian at all accurately, that's a document that comes from the 3rd Army, isn't it, from the commander of the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: From the command of the 3rd Army --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Yes. And if you look down at 248, entry 2, that's a document from the command of the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And they both start with a file number 872, don't they?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So one explanation for this mystery we're dealing with here today is that whoever made this entry simply put that second document in the wrong place and it should have been up as a 247, number 2, since they related in both documents from the 3rd Army, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: That type of mistake is possible; however, here, if you allow me, we have something else that is to be observed. Number 872 indicates, since it is the same number, that it comes from the 3rd Army and the command of the 3rd Army is a forward command post. So that is a way of filing it that we call a list of documents. So -94 could not have been created before the document under 137 because they are kept in chronological order in the list of documents, if we see that things are done in accordance with the rules on office work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That would be true if these came from exactly the same source, but they don't. The one under 248 comes from the forward command post, the one from 247 comes from the command. The document sequence at the command is different from the document sequence at the command post; isn't that true, or do you not know that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I based my knowledge or conclusions on the rules on office work. 872 is at the command of the army and the forward command post. In principle, that is not possible because these are two lists of documents in two different places and the subnumber is the same. If it is one list of documents, then chronologically one sees that first it is document 137 that was created, and after that on the 26th of May document 94 was created, which physically cannot be matched that way in the list of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Unless you're incorrect regarding the difference between forward command post documents and documents that come from the command in Pec, and I suggest to you that you are. Now, let me ask you then to go back to 3D1108, and if you look at the fourth column, log number and date, and try to find document 247, I think you'll fail to find it, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: On page 1, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, in any of the pages. Look at all the pages. Do you see 247 anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you maybe conclude that that document must be between number 7 and number 78 somewhere?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Lots of things can be assumed, but I cannot be certain. In principle, that is where it should be in it was supposed to be destroyed or, I beg your pardon, archived. In view of the fact that it says "keep permanently," I assume that it should be between these two numbers, 7 and 78.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you've conceded to me so far that mistakes in making these entries are possible, and you've talked about several mistakes today. You talked about a mistake made by a typist who put in the name Radomir Ristic instead of Svetislav Ristic in paragraph 9 of your statement we see that and in your testimony today. You talked about mistakes made by the Ministry of Justice with regard to documents 3D1090 and 3D788, and you talked about a mistake made in document 3D00639 where you said what you had said was not recorded correctly. So mistakes seem to be fairly common, don't they, just in the small portion -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Ever since this involves a longer period of time, conditions that were not pleasant at all, work conditions, that is to say there was an imminent threat of bombing, then there was the bombing itself, it is possible that mistakes happen. However, in this case it has to do with a few mistakes that are simply too many for one particular place and one particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In paragraph 14 of your statement, you talk about a -- this registry of documents. Can you tell us -- these would be documents coming into your office on a daily basis. Can you tell me how many documents on the average would come into that office every day that would have to be dealt with by this registry?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have the exact numbers, but on average it was at least around ten documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Only ten from the 1st Army, 2nd Army, 3rd Army, army, navy, you would only get ten documents a day?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I said at least ten, which is to say that in some periods it could have been 20 and in others less than ten. The dynamics were very, very variable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: "At least" in English doesn't convey the meaning that the witness has now given us. You would expect that to be on average ten documents, if it could be more than ten or less than ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would ten be an average; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to reconstruct, or rather, divide the number of documents by the number of days. Well, perhaps it could be put that way, on average about ten documents; but one should bear in mind that certain documents, especially those of an urgent nature that was supposed to be signed by the Chief of General Staff, were brought in to him by the assistant chiefs. I am talking about the mail that we prepared regularly in the morning and in the afternoon, there were two particular times, when we submitted those to the Chief of General Staff for his signature. A number of documents did not have the nature of an order and did not have to be presented to the Chief of General Staff. That was resolved by certain tactical leaders or desk officers in the cabinet or office. The Chief of General Staff during the regular signing was just informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Once again we're failing to communicate and it's probably my fault. The documents I'm trying to get you to tell me about are those that you speak about in paragraph 14 of your statement, and in that paragraph you talk about documents that are received by your office and you talk about reports and correspondence and all kinds of things coming in there. And I'm wondering not how many documents go out of your office each day but how many come in at that time.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: It's the way I put it, the way I said. Can I say at least or on average around ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want you to look at P1459, that's the first document in your folder there. At paragraph 16 of your statement you speak about being shown this document, and with regard to that you say this: "On inspection of the document I can say that I do not remember the content of the document nor can I confirm that it was received in the office because there's not one technical indication of it. There is no received stamp, entry number, or any annotation by the Chief of the General Staff on the document." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, the first thing I want to ask you about is in the top centre of the document you see the numbers 81/3 with a circle around them. Do you know what that means?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: In this case, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in the right-hand -- upper right-hand corner you see the number 72, which I think we've learned today is a registry number, a document registry number for some registry; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The filing number of the document is inscribed in that way only if the filing stamp is on the last page, so that even without opening the document one could see under which number it was registered. If the filing number is on the first page then this annotation is not placed, what document that is, but here there is no stamp either. That is the way in which a person who works with documents, by leafing through documents, can find a document easy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that prompts maybe a series of questions. Well, it certainly was not uncommon in your office for General Ojdanic to issue orders that would go to 1st Army, 2nd Army, 3rd Army, air force, and navy, five different places, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: An order is submitted and was submitted in accordance with the signature at the end of the document. It is possible that it was done by the commander of the strategic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know what's happening. I don't know whether you're not -- my questions aren't be translated properly or you're not listening or what. My question is this: General Ojdanic would on occasion draft an order that was to go to the 1st Army, the 2nd Army, the 3rd Army, the air force, and the navy, five different places, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm listening to you carefully, and that is how I understood the question, and yes, the order is sent to five addresses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And each of those addresses then has some kind of a system by which they stamp it that it was received or make some notation on it that it was received or give it a number or something, don't they?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: According to the rules on office work, that is compulsory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: A document has to be recorded as an incoming document by way of a stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when you tell us that you don't recall seeing P1459 and you think you didn't because it has no received stamp on it, that probably means it didn't come to your office but went to some other office. And if you now look at 3D1106, which is the document that did come to your office, it does have the received stamp from your office on it, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: There is a received stamp, and the document was received on the 26th and as for the way in which it reached the cabinet it was supposed to be logged under a new number because it has nothing to do with the document of the Ministry of Defence. However, it was logged under 248, subnumber 2, on the 26th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you were also shown a document 4D135 by Mr. Visnjic just a few moments ago, and you had occasion to go through that document. I have not provided you a copy of it, but this is a document listing requests made by the 3rd Army and the disposition of those requests, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is an analysis of the realisation of the requests of the commander of the 3rd Army, or rather, requests, what was done with these requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And could we go to, like, I think maybe the second page in the English and the Serbian -- no, the next page, third page. There we go. I think we need to go back one page, maybe. Rather than take a bunch of time trying to find exactly what I'm looking for -- here we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This talks about here on this page it talks about some unapproved, unimplemented or partially unimplemented requests. And just as an example there's one request resubordination of a special brigade, there's one request replenishment with some tanks, one that requests replenishment with a mechanised company, a request for replenishment, another request for replenishment, another request to add two command posts, proposal to appoint judge jurists to the military court. This is all things that the 3rd Army was making requests for, things that the 3rd Army wanted to be supplied with or appointments to be made or things of that nature. Now, this document that we're looking at 3D1105 isn't -- sorry, 3D1106, this isn't any request, this isn't: Give me more troops, give me more tanks, this is a report. This is a report on the failure of an order to be carried out and a report about things that are going on. He's not making a request there, so it wouldn't be in this list of requests of having been dealt with, would it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: What I see is the Serbian version of page 1. I don't know see that particular paragraph. If this wasn't a request, perhaps you should ask whoever produced this piece of analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, this -- this particular document, 3D1106, is not mentioned in that list of requests, is it, it wasn't a request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's very difficult for me to use all these legal indications, so to speak, so I have to take some time and track this down, the right reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question you're being asked is whether you would expect the document that you're looking at, the analysis of requests, whether you would expect that to contain the report that is the subject of this evidence, and Mr. Ackerman is suggesting you wouldn't expect it in there. So what's your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my assessment, it shouldn't be part of the analysis of requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, let's go back to 3D1106 again, and I want to direct your attention now to paragraph 3 and paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but I can't see the left-hand half of the page. If we could please scroll to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I just want to draw your attention to what it is that General Pavkovic is reporting there. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't see the left side of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think you have it in your book there, if you look at 3D1106 in your book you'll be able to see it better probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, we're going to have to interrupt you at some stage, so let's do it now if that's not too much inconvenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine. I didn't realise we were at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We are. And just before leaving the courtroom can I ask Mr. Visnjic one question. In paragraph 16 of the statement it says that document 1459 is more or less the same as 1724. That is, in fact, a third version of this document, is it? Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, these are both documents that the OTP subsumed under the same number, but it's one and the same document. They gave two numbers to one document; that's actually what I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it's not more or less the same, it's identical, it's identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll resume -- sorry. Mr. Vlajkovic, we need to have a break for half an hour. Could you please leave with the usher again and we'll resume at ten to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For urgent personal reasons, Judge Nosworthy will not be with us for this last session, but we shall continue on the basis that we consider it to be in the interests of justice to do so. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I, with your leave, just indicate that in respect to the matter you raised just before the court rose last, 1724 and 1459 are identical documents, both bearing P numbers, both received from differently sources on different dates. 1459 was received in a batch of documents handed over to the OTP by Prime Minister Djindjic and Mr. -- And General Pavkovic, and 14 -- and 1724 was received by us pursuant to a response to an RFA, an RFA being a request for assistance, from the Government of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Colonel, I've had you look at 3D1106, 3D1106, yes, and the contents of that document. I want you to look now at another document, this one is 4D192.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And while we are getting to it may I just add for the record 4D192 is the same document as P1458, which was admitted on the 20th of March this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at this document, it's a 24 May 1999 document from the Pristina Corps command to the 3rd Army command, and it's called a report on the failure to execute the order to resubordinate MUP forces. Paragraph 2 you see that General Lazarevic reports that MUP forces have not been subordinated as the order requires. In paragraph 6 he talks about the problems at the check-points and the MUP crimes against the civilian population. I think you'll agree with me that basically what he's reporting here is the same information that General Pavkovic then included in his report of the very next day, 25 May, which he then sent up to your office, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I've been able to see, that may be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, as the chief of the chef de cabinet for General Ojdanic, I'm sure you were aware, were you not, of some meetings that were held in Belgrade on the 16th and the 17th of May, 1999, between General Ojdanic and General Pavkovic and General Lukic and others on the 16th, and then finally ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry it wasn't Lukic, it was Vasiljevic. General Lukic wasn't there. It was held on the 16th of May and then a meeting with Slobodan Milosevic and General Ojdanic and General Pavkovic and others on the 17th of May where the subject was: Reports of crimes being committed in Kosovo. You're aware of those two meetings, weren't you, as chief of cabinet?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I did not go into what was actually discussed at those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What do you mean you didn't go into it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think what specific issues were raised at the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it was about these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: General Ojdanic didn't tell you what those meetings were about?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: On this particular occasion, no, I don't think he did. I can't remember the issues that were raised at those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I have another document now I'd like you to look at, it's P1696. This is a document dated 4 May 1999 and it's a report of something that was published apparently by RTS in Belgrade, and it speaks of meeting, if you look down -- look at the top, a meeting attended by General Pavkovic, Major-General Lukic, Slobodan Milosevic, where matters going on in Kosovo were discussed. And if you look further down in the story it reports that among the things that were discussed was this: "The security forces dealt with numerous cases of violence, killings, pillage, and other crimes arresting several hundred perpetrators whose crimes were a great danger to the civilian population. The state authorities legally and in an unbiased manner carried out their duties notably the protection of the citizens' personal security and the security of their property. It was concluded that these measures had made such actions impossible. Military courts acting in accordance with the proceedings envisaged in war conditions have already passed a large number of sentences ranging from 5 to 20 years' imprisonment for the crimes committed." And I can tell you that a nearly identical report also appeared in Politika on the same day, on the 5th of May. Now, my question is: Were you aware of these press reports and aware of this meeting that was attended by General Ojdanic where this was discussed and reported publicly?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: There are several issues involved here. So first and foremost I must --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Listen to my question. My question is: Were you aware of these press reports of this meeting and General Ojdanic's attendance at this meeting? That's what I want an answer to. I don't want you to tell me a bunch of issues involved.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think General Ojdanic, Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, attended this meeting, but I did not follow media reports at the time and I don't know what the printed media specifically were claiming. I simply had no time to analyse the media --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've answered the question. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 24 of your statement to this Tribunal you say this: "At collegium meetings and briefings there were no reports of war crimes of any kind until early June 1999." Now, can you explain to us why it was General Ojdanic failed to tell the collegium about the meeting on the 5th of May, about the meetings on the 16th and 17th of May, why did he withhold that information from the collegium and why did he not take steps to remedy those situations? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The regular briefings that were held during the war were mostly about briefings by the assistant chiefs of the General Staff, and this was normally about issues with regard to the previous period of time or that particular day on which the meeting took place. I can't really say why General Ojdanic had never done any briefings about that, but the fact is at the collegium meetings at the time the war crimes issue was not raised until the beginning of June, as I said in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you knew, didn't you, that that was an important issue that was being discussed in the western press and an issue was being made about it, and my question to you that you didn't answer is: Do you know why General Ojdanic failed to take steps to deal with that and failed to report it to the collegium? Do you know why? You can say no. If you don't know why, just say you don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I think the meeting was actually the 4th of May; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it was, Your Honour, the Politika report was the 5th, the RTS report was the 4th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Ackerman, I have just a question or a query to make. One way of getting into this type of information which you are seeking is to -- and the witness said that he knows nothing about why this was withheld from the collegium, is to make a suggestion to the

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: didn't, that's another thing. If you know of the reason, would you like to make that suggestion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. I wish I did know the reason, I don't, and I don't want to just guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I just have a few matters I would like to clarify with you.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Starting with a couple matters in your statement. At paragraph 16 of your statement in the last sentence, the last and the second-to-last sentence you speak about 4D135 and you say that: "On the basis of the document's content I can confirm that all three of the 3rd Army requests were recorded, irrespective of whether they came through the office or through the people responsible for taking practical [indiscernible]." What is it you mean when you say "all three of the 3rd Army requests"?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: It's not about all three requests. All requests of the 3rd Army, that's what it says, regardless of whether they got there through the cabinet or through the tactical focal points. It's not about all three requests, it's about the requests of the 3rd Army. So this may be a translation problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I see. So if you -- you were shown some documents, the contents of which are the same, P1459 and 3D1106, in the last page or last sentence in that document you see there is a request or a recommendation made by General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps we could look at the document. Let's look at Exhibit 3D1106, last paragraph of the document, if we could go there, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Recommended measures and it says: "It is necessary for the Supreme Command to take urgent steps within its powers to resubordinate the units and organs of the MUP of Serbia, abiding by the spirit of the constitution and existing laws and in accordance with the proclaimed state of war or to rescind the order on their resubordination and as it has done so far leave control and command of the forces of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia to the Ministry of the Interior - the staff of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia for Kosovo and Metohija through the Joint Command." Do you see that? The question is --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Stamp, but I seem unable to pin-point that paragraph. I'm afraid we're talking about different documents. 3D --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you look at the document on your screen, can you read the last paragraph of the document on your screen?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, all right, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You have read those recommendations, sir. The question is this: Were the recommendations you see set out in that paragraph, would you expect those to be included in the list of requests from the 3rd Army that were not implemented that you saw in document 4D135?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: It wouldn't be unfounded if that, too, was included in the analysis, but the issues that do get analysed is something that the team leader decides. He analysed the written requests of the 3rd Army command. Why was this specifically not included in the analysis is definitely not something that I can comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Another thing I'd like to clarify about your statement is that at paragraph 18, and this is P -- sorry, this is Exhibit 3D1112. Do you have paragraph 18 there, sir, of your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: My statement? I can't see it on the screen, but, yes, I do have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the second paragraph of paragraph 18 you speak of recording the minutes of the briefings, but immediately after that you go on to say: "After the collegium these tasks were updated and specified." What I'd really like to know is whether or not you are speaking in this paragraph about briefings, daily briefings, collegium meetings, or both, firstly.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Both, in the briefest possible terms, because this aspect, however, control over members of the General Staff was referred in peacetime -- was referred to in peacetime as collegium meetings and in wartime these were referred to as briefings, but essentially it's the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you spoke specifically about collegium sessions and the recording of those sessions at paragraph 6 of your statement and paragraph 7. I'll just read the relevant parts. You say: "Sessions of the collegium were recorded and later typed up in a restricted area." And in paragraph 7 you said: "The recording on disk is sent to the chief of office and is archived in the registry." Paragraph 8: "A specific number of tapes are used for recording the sessions of the collegium," and there you reference specifically to collegium sessions. What I want to know if we turn to paragraph 18 is whether or not this method of making the records you say: "Minutes were kept at all the briefings and analyses. The minutes were handwritten in a thick A4 notebook." Does that apply to collegium sessions or can you clarify from what appears to be a discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The meetings of the collegium of the Chief of the General Staff that were held before the beginning of the war were tape recorded in the way described in the statement. As for briefings during wartime, which were in actual fact meetings of the collegium of the General Staff, those were not tape recorded. Minutes were taken. The technical conditions were not in place for tape-recordings to be made. In these cases, the minutes were used as a basis for any assignments that were determined and for the distribution of those assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who took the minutes of those briefings?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The focal point for the drafting of the minutes in the written form was the operative sector of the administration of the staff of the Supreme Command. Those taking the minutes were Paskas Dragan and Mucibabic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you repeat the name, the last name you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Dragan Paskas and Colonel Spasoje Mucibabic. They normally took the minutes during wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So as chief of the office, did you check the minutes against your notes?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I checked only whenever I needed to check something or if the conclusions weren't clearly phrased. I wasn't one to go through the entire set of minutes just in order to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were the minutes confirmed at the next succeeding briefing?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. At the next briefing I would inform concerning the implementation of tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we look at 3D728 -- sorry, I withdraw that. I'm asking for 3D580.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You can see there that those -- this document indicates that it is the briefing -- or the minutes of the briefing for the 26th of March, 1999. Is that the format of the minutes of the briefing that you are familiar with?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: By its format and by the content, it differs from previous briefings, first because it was held at 8.00 in the morning; and secondly, because it was chaired by or conducted by Lieutenant-General Obradovic -- or Colonel-General Obradovic, and first it was a briefing at the operations administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The English copy says the meeting was at 8.30 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The beginning at 08 -- or 0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The English also says that it ended at 2200 hours. Are we looking at the same document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think I need to clarify that and perhaps we could move on while an effort is made to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that if we look at page 2 then it would correspond to the English translation. I'm confused as to why this happened. I don't know. But I think the second page of the document in the B/C/S, if he has it, would correspond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, probably the first page of the document was not translated, so now it would correspond to what ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vlajkovic, you'll see the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now -- so the -- if we could go back to the question that you were asked: Is this the format of the minutes of the briefing that you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. This format is something that I saw during preparations for my testimony, and it's an excerpt from the minutes from the original book where the actual minutes were taken by hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you say "excerpt," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Not excerpt, but typed as is written in the actual minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, can you have a look at the last page of this document, and that is page 4 in the English, the last page, last line. We see General Ojdanic speaking and he says -- he's reported to say: "Make a map for me to the Supreme Defence Council." Is that as you said earlier in your previous answer typed as it is written in the actual minutes?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: This cannot be determined unless one looks at the minutes, the original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could look at 3D5 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move off that. That -- the instruction at the end that's just been read to you, does it make sense?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It makes sense if we're talking about a map indicating the forces, or rather, most probably, the Chief of the General Staff specifically mentioned which map but the minute-taker did not note that down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the original version of these handwritten an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour -- well, Mr. Visnjic can probably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, 3D1094.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we have a look at 3D581.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is a -- the minutes of a briefing on the 28th of March, two days later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we look at page 3 of the English, which is top of page 4 in the B/C/S you see - and I can indicate that this appears to be General Gajic speaking - and he is saying: "I support General Grahovac's proposal to make an assessment in the presence of the Supreme Defence Council members."

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't have that part of the text here. I'm looking at the Serbian version -- oh, yes, it's here. Yes, I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you are not -- well, I'll ask you this: Did you know of the Supreme Defence Council meeting at that time, the 26th and the 28th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The Supreme Defence Council. I cannot be definite about whether it was held or not because it was held at a location where the supreme defence staff was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that there's been some confusion, perhaps the witness can reply to this question again, but I can see from the transcript that evidently ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you talking about the reference to supreme defence staff or are you talking -- or are you thinking -- well, I have assumed that was Supreme Command Staff. Please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were aware of the Supreme Command, I take it, that existed or a body called the Supreme Command that existed during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The term "Supreme Command" was used in communication amongst ourselves, yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think it's accepted from your statement that General Ojdanic was the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command Staff. When he attended meetings of the Supreme Command, did you ever go with him? Did you ever attend any meeting of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In terms of your experience and your knowledge of the operations of the office and the agenda of General Ojdanic, are you able to say who were the members of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: According to my understanding, let's say, of the Supreme Command, by the nature of things for me that was the Supreme Defence Council, which during the war let's say acquired the name "Supreme Command." The president of the republic, so of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, with the two republican presidents, Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said according to your understanding. How did you arrive at this understanding?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia defines the control of the Army of Yugoslavia in peacetime, that is the Supreme Defence Council. At the beginning of the war when the term "Supreme Command" was mentioned, I -- what was meant I thought was the Supreme Defence Council in the composition of the three presidents or in its expanded composition, then also it would be attended by the minister of internal affairs, the Chief of the General Staff, and then some other governmental organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, in your capacity as chief of the office -- or is your understanding consistent with documents you would have seen and discussions that you would have been present at in your capacity as chief of the office of General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Documents that we worked on would be passed on to the military cabinet of the president of the republic, which we addressed as Mr. President and president of the Supreme Defence Council at the beginning of the war. In the beginning of April, the chief of the military cabinet, General Susic, the chief of the military cabinet of the president of the republic suggested to me that the documents should be addressed to the supreme commander, or rather, we would be sending it through the military cabinet for information or so that the supreme commander could be informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, what I'm asking you, though, is you said based on your understanding of the membership of the Supreme Command is based to some extent on your understanding of the constitution. What I'm asking you is: Practically speaking, was there any knowledge or experience that you gained from your position of as chief of General Ojdanic's office that confirmed your knowledge as to the composition of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Later, yes, because we meant by that the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was it later that confirmed your understanding? And I take it that your understanding is that the membership of the Supreme Defence Council became the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The fact that the question was not completely resolved in legal terms and what I said at the beginning, our understanding of that organ was that that was the Supreme Command. No other specific act or move.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we look quickly at P -- sorry, 5D -- 3D, 3D728.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you have it there? You will see under --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That purports to be the record of a briefing of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command of the 11th of April. Let's go to the last page, last paragraph of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think maybe it's my mistake. Is this 3D728? I'm asking for 3D728.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is 3D728, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm in a moment of consternation. That is -- and is this the last page of 3D728?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, it is the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think I'll have to clarify this and move on because -- I'll get back to that, Your Honours. I apologise for ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I ask you, though, sir, in the meetings of the Supreme Command Staff, do you know whether or not Mr. Milutinovic ever attended?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Not meetings of the Supreme Command Staff, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What meetings are you aware that he attended?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can just judge by the nature of the function that he attended meetings of the Supreme Defence Council, but not the Supreme Command Staff, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know of him attending any meetings of the Supreme Command during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know of Mr. Sainovic attending any meeting of the Supreme Command before the war [as said]?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not attend those meetings and I don't know who attended them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could return to Exhibit P728 and I should explain that the -- Exhibit 3D728, and we are going to page 3, not the last page. Apparently somehow it's the last page on the copy I have, but I have been advised that it's actually page 3 in English and which also corresponds to page 3 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see at the bottom of that page General Ojdanic speaks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have a remark on the transcript. My knowledge of English being such, line -- actually, page 83, line 10, Mr. Stamped asked - I don't know why - if Mr. Sainovic attended meetings of the Supreme Command before the war and during the war, and what was recorded was just before the war, but he answered as well for -- during the war and the witness said that he did not know who attended that -- the meetings. That would be it, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you accept that, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, please proceed with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you read there what we have General Ojdanic saying in the minutes of this briefing.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: "During the evening amend the directive in line with ours." And then the second item would be: "Submit the draft plan for study, the briefing will be at 0900 hours with the supreme commander, present deputy operations and staff affairs, chief of the operations administration, chief of the Supreme Command Staff, Lieutenant-General Smiljanic, Major-General Krga, President Milosevic, President Milutinovic, and adjutant of the MUP unit for Kosovo Sreten -- Sreten, Vice-President Sainovic and Colonel-General Pavkovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you read that record of the briefing, does that refresh your recollection as to who the membership of the supreme -- or what the membership of the Supreme Command was as of the 11th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can it not wait, Mr. Petrovic? Can we wait -- is it something to do with the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's important about what the witness heard, which translation he heard and the translation Mr. Stamp received of the witness's previous answer. So it's page 84, line 14. Your Honours, it's very important, in view of the characterisation of the organ that the witness is talking about and that is mentioned here. The witness interpreted the abbreviation in one way and it's being translated in a different way. This is the gist of it. I do not want to be explicit, but it's clear what the organ is talked about. Here there is mention of the organ, but the witness actually spoke about an individual. So I don't want to be too explicit, but the abbreviation VK the witness read as the supreme commander and not as the Supreme Command, as it is stated in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but are you saying the English translation is wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the document the translation is wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would have been much easier if you would have just said that to me --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you permit, the witness said "supreme commander," the witness said "supreme commander," and not "Supreme Command." So I'm not talking about the document; I'm talking about what the witness said, and this can be easily established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness read the document. Now, are you saying he's read it wrongly?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm saying that he was reading the document and that in reading the document the abbreviation VK he read out at "vrhovni komandant," supreme commander, this is what the witness said and that can be established by listening back to the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I take it from your answer that you are saying that that abbreviation can be translated either way, it can be referred to by a witness speaking Serbian as either "Supreme Command" or "supreme commander"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do not dare interpret military abbreviations. This is something that we need to ask the witness. My intervention only refers to what the witness said and what it says in the transcript, but the witness knows what the abbreviation is and what that means. I'm not going any further than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vlajkovic, you've read a passage there which has the letters PK. What do you say these represent?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, it's VK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My mistake. The letters VK, what do you say these represent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] VK stands for supreme commander; if we're talking about the Supreme Command, then it would be indicated with VK-DA, "vrhovna komanda." This is how we differentiate in military terminology between commander and command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stamp, what's your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, with the leave of the Court perhaps I could ask it tomorrow, but before I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I thought you were nearly finished and we were letting it run in the hope that you were. But have you got long to go? There's no case here this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I could finish this afternoon but I've about ten minutes to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ten minutes. Unless I hear howls of anguish from the interpreters, in view of the fact there's no case this afternoon, I think it would be helpful to all if we could continue. Okay. We seem to have the thumbs up. Please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before I get back to my last question, your last answer was that VK stands for supreme commander; and if you're talking about Supreme Command, then it would be VK-DA.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see in the document I showed you a list of names that is said to be present. Do you know what that list is referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I mean, for once one should read properly. This is a reading problem not a legal problem. Mr. Stamp says this is a list of persons who --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't understand Mr. Fila. We're sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, the interpreters didn't understand what you were saying; could you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said Mr. Stamp's question got the wrong tense. He's asking the witness to say that these persons were present, which is the past tense, and this is a question in reference to the future tense. And the witness cannot know whether someone in the future was present or will be present, will be present, that's what I'm saying, tomorrow. You see tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, your question, in my opinion, is perfectly valid and you should proceed to ask it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: These -- this list of names, do you, as someone who was the chief of office who regularly attends these briefings, know what this list of names is referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: These are amendments to the directive or a draft plan that the chief will be briefing the supreme commander on the next day at 9.00, who should attend or will attend from the army, the chief of operations and staff affairs, the chief of the Operative Command, the chief of the Supreme Command Staff, General Ojdanic; Lieutenant-General Smiljanic, as commander of the air force and air defence, and Major-General Krga; as well as President Milosevic, Milutinovic, and the adjutant of the MUP units for Kosovo, did they attend, well I -- but the chief said that they might attend the briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: According to your knowledge and experience as chief of office, did these people - and I'm referring to the civilians listed here - regularly attend briefings by the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was they, some others, or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have it here that you just said: "I don't know whether it was they, some others, or ..." Can you just say or what you said.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Or -- or who could possibly attend. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. In the -- if I may move on to something else very quickly. In the course of your experience as chief of the office, did you see documents sent to or received from a body called the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Not a single document reached the cabinet from the Supreme Command. In our communication with the supreme commander we spoke through the chief of the military cabinet --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think there might be a misunderstanding here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we look at P1487.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we look at the stamps at the bottom of the -- or the signatures at the bottom of the document that appears on page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you see the bottom of that document and tell us whether or not you can say if that is a document that was sent out by General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could return to the first page in English. It's dated the 17th of April, 1999, addressed to the command of the 3rd Army personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we make some progress, Mr. Stamp, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was just waiting for the translation to -- very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see it says: "Link: Kosovo and Metohija Joint Command order strictly confidential number 455-148 of 15 April 1999." Can you recall ever seeing this document before?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: This document I have not seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: If I'm expected to comment --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I just want to know if you have ever seen it before. It -- this document which you said was sent by General Ojdanic refers to an order of the Joint Command. Now, the question is: Had you ever seen within your capacity as chief of General Ojdanic's office documents made by or sent to an organ called the Joint Command, Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999 I did not see any such documents. No such documents went through the register of the cabinet. This document was produced in the sector for operations and staff affairs. It was meant to be sent in any encrypted form and it was an urgent document, and I said this was one of the ways where the focal point in such cases took this directly to the chief for his signature, and it was distributed as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So I take it, it follows from that, that there were documents issued by your office which you did not see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Mr. President, this document was not issued by my office, it was issued by the sector for operations and staff affairs, the operative administration; and as such, it was entered into their register, it's in their files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question was badly phrased. This is the sort of document that might be issued from the Supreme Command Staff without you seeing it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Documents produced by focal points of an urgent nature, or rather, documents that did not wait for the regular procedure in order to be signed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not get the last portion of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I have nothing further for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I see that the interpreters didn't get the last portion of the witness's answer, and the witness said, morning and afternoon, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do have questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How long do you anticipate?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In English, since it hasn't come up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that will need to be tomorrow then. Mr. Vlajkovic, we have to finish for the day at this stage. You will have to come back tomorrow to complete your evidence, that will be at 9.00 tomorrow morning. Between then and now, please have no discussion or communication with anyone at all about the evidence in this case. Please keep off the subject completely no matter who you speak to. Now please leave the courtroom with the usher and we'll see you at 9.00 tomorrow.
